steps.title: Participle clauses
steps.html:
What they are. A participle clause replaces a full clause with a single verb form, dropping both the subject and the conjunction: Because they had lived through two recessions, they were cautious becomes Having lived through two recessions, they were cautious. They belong to written English and to careful speech; they make a text shorter and, used badly, make it ambiguous.

Three forms. The -ing participle is active and means as / because / and: Wanting a stable job, she stayed. The -ed participle is passive and usually means when / because / although: Asked about it, they agreed. The perfect participle (having done, having been done) marks the earlier of two events: Having been told twice, he left.

The one hard rule. The unstated subject of the participle must be the subject of the main clause. Asked about the survey, the results were surprising claims that the results were asked. Either change the main clause (Asked about the survey, the researchers said the results were surprising) or use a full clause.

Reduced relative clauses. The same forms shorten relative clauses: the people who work here → the people working here; the answer which was given by a young worker → the answer given by a young worker. Only defining clauses with be can be reduced this way.

Keeping the conjunction. Some conjunctions can stay in front for clarity: while working abroad, before leaving, after being told, when asked. This is common and often clearer.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• A dangling participle: Walking home, the rain started.
  • Active for passive: Asking about it, they agreed when they were the ones asked.
  • Keeping the subject: Having they lived through it, they were cautious.
  • Using a participle where the subjects differ: Being late, the meeting started without me.
  • Two participles stacked with no punctuation, so nobody can find the main verb.

steps.title: Text A · What everybody knows
steps.html:
Written for this course.

Everybody knows the descriptions. Born between 1965 and 1980, Gen X are easy-going, family-focused and deeply suspicious of employers. Gen Y are fussy about who they work for, enthusiastic about the work itself and unimpressed by job titles. Gen Z, arriving last, are said to be either the most rebellious cohort in decades or the most conventional, depending on which article you happen to be reading; keen on stable jobs, optimistic about their own lives and pessimistic about everything else, they are described in terms that are supposed to be characteristic of a generation raised online. Asked to describe themselves, members of all three groups reach for the same words: open-minded, realistic, hard-working. Asked about the group below them, they become noticeably less generous, producing self-centred and arrogant within about a minute.

There is a labelling problem underneath all of this. Described by a manager who is sympathetic towards them, a young employee asking for feedback is self-confident; described by one who is not, the same employee is arrogant. Keen on flexible hours, they are either realistic about modern life or not loyal enough, and which of those you write down says more about you than about them.

We associate impatience with the young because we stop noticing it in ourselves, and the same answer, given by a twenty-year-old, is coded differently from the way it is coded when a fifty-year-old gives it. None of this is deliberate. It is what happens when a category is available and a judgement has to be made quickly, and it is the reason the descriptions in the first paragraph feel so obviously true to almost everybody who reads them.

steps.title: Text B · What the evidence shows
steps.html:
Written for this course, from Costanza, Badger, Fraser, Severt & Gade, Journal of Business and Psychology 27(4), 2012.

Being confident about something is not the same as being right about it. In 2012 a team of researchers collected twenty published and unpublished studies covering nearly twenty thousand employees, comparing four generations on three things that organisations actually care about: job satisfaction, commitment to the employer, and intention to leave. Combining the studies statistically, they found differences that were small to moderate and, in many of the comparisons, essentially zero. Their conclusion was blunt: meaningful generational differences in these attitudes probably do not exist.

Understanding why the belief survives means separating three things that a single survey cannot separate. The first is age: people are different at twenty-five from how they are at fifty, whatever year they were born. The second is period — a recession or a housing crisis hits everybody at once, regardless of cohort. The third is generation proper. Run a survey in one year and all three arrive tangled together, and the tidiest explanation is usually the one that gets printed. The categories are also commercially useful, which is a different thing from being accurate: a birth year is easier to sell than a personality, and, having been repeated for thirty years, the labels now feel like observations rather than inventions.

What survives the criticism is modest but real. Shared events do shape people, and somebody who left university in 2009 entered a labour market that somebody leaving in 2006 never saw. But the boundaries are arbitrary — December 1980 and January 1981 are not two different worlds — and the variation inside any generation is far larger than the gap between them. Taken seriously, the research does not say that people are all alike. It says the dividing line is almost certainly not the year of birth.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
People born in the early 1990s are accused, usually by people twenty years older, of being fussy about employers and not loyal to anybody. Asked about it directly, most of them agree with the first half and find the second half strange, since nobody has offered them anything to be loyal to.

The fair part is the fussiness. Having watched an older cousin work eleven years for a company that closed the office by email, they treat the words “we are a family here” as a warning rather than an offer. I have sat in three interviews where the candidate asked about turnover before asking about salary, which would have been unthinkable in 2005.

What is not fair is self-centred. The same people organise leaving parties, cover each other’s shifts and answer messages at eleven at night. Described as difficult by managers who have never asked them a question, they are in my experience easy-going about almost everything except being lied to.

The accusation, I think, is really about power. Being fussy about who you work for is characteristic of anybody with a choice, and this is the first group in thirty years that has had one. We associate that with arrogance because we are not used to hearing it from people who are twenty-nine.
